description:
We are a team of students from Sehriyo School who love space, science, and technology. We are creating MARS MISSION LAB, an educational game where children explore Mars, drive a rover, collect resources, and learn how people could live on Mars.

Our goal is to make learning science fun and exciting. Our team is already formed, but we are happy to share ideas and learn from others.
summary:
MARS MISSION LAB is a free, browser-based educational game in which a student becomes an engineer who prepares a base on Mars before the first people arrive. The player drives a rover, scans the terrain, finds water ice and regolith, brings them to the base, builds new modules, and produces oxygen and water. The player must also manage the rover's energy and the dust on the solar panels.

The game addresses three educational challenges: access to STEM education is not equal for everyone, students should become interested in science long before university, and theory alone is not enough without practice. It is free, needs no installation, and lets students learn by doing: every decision has consequences, and scientific facts based on NASA resources (SWIM subsurface ice mapping, the MOXIE oxygen experiment, the Mars Fact Sheet) appear during play. Our goal is to inspire the next generation of scientists and engineers.
details:
WHAT IT IS

MARS MISSION LAB is a free educational browser game in which a student becomes an engineer who prepares a base on Mars before the first people arrive. The player drives a rover, scans the terrain, finds water ice and regolith (Martian soil), mines them and brings them to the base. Regolith is turned into building blocks, ice is turned into water, and oxygen can be produced in two ways: by electrolysis of water and from Martian carbon dioxide, following the principle of NASA's MOXIE experiment. The player decides where to go, what to mine and what to build, while keeping an eye on the rover's energy and on the dust that covers the solar panels and reduces electricity production.

PROBLEMS IT SOLVES AND BENEFITS

- Accessibility: not every student has access to good STEM education. The game is free and runs directly in the browser, with nothing to install.

- Interest in science: instead of reading a text about Mars, the student drives the rover, explores the planet and builds a base. This helps spark interest in science before university.

- Practice: theory alone is not enough. In the game every decision has consequences (a drained rover, dusty panels), so the player learns to think like an engineer. Scientific facts appear right during gameplay.

EXPECTED IMPACT

We want any student to be able to understand, in a playful way, why Mars needs ice, energy and oxygen and what it means to use resources on site (ISRU). In the future we plan to add new buildings and new missions.

TOOLS AND TECHNOLOGIES

The game is written in HTML, CSS and JavaScript and runs in an ordinary browser on a computer, with no extra hardware or software. The scientific basis comes from NASA SWIM (subsurface ice mapping), the MOXIE experiment on the Perseverance rover and the NASA Mars Fact Sheet.

CREATIVITY

We turned a complex topic into a clear gameplay loop: scan, mine, transport, build. The student does not just read about Martian resources, but goes through the whole path from finding ice to producing oxygen and water. The game includes a "Mars Laboratory" with scientific facts, and the look of the buildings is inspired by NASA research.

FACTORS OUR TEAM CONSIDERED

- Scientific accuracy: the facts are based on NASA materials. Where real numbers are too small (for example, MOXIE produced only 122 grams of oxygen in total), we state openly that the values in the game are increased and simplified for playability.

- Realism: the game follows the ISRU principle, but some equipment still has to be brought from Earth.

- Simplicity and accessibility: free, no installation and a clear interface for students.

- This is an educational project, not an official NASA product.
